question: A 45-year-old man with suspected pemphigus has extensive trunk erosions and painful oral ulcers preventing him from eating or drinking. What is the most appropriate primary management before dermatology referral?

answers.text: Non-adherent wound care, fluid and electrolyte monitoring with replacement, analgesic mouthwash and nutritional support, infection surveillance, consider short-course bridging prednisolone, and arrange urgent referral

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Extensive erosions in pemphigus behave like partial-thickness burns: the patient loses fluid, protein, and electrolytes and is at high risk of sepsis. Primary management is supportive — gentle non-adherent dressings, fluid replacement, nutritional support, infection watch, and pain relief — with a short bridging corticosteroid if needed, followed by urgent specialist referral.

answers.text: Apply adhesive tape dressings firmly over the erosions and discharge with oral antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adhesive tape on fragile perilesional skin in pemphigus will shear off more epidermis and extend the erosions. Dressings must be non-adherent. Discharging without fluid assessment, nutritional support, or specialist referral risks life-threatening dehydration and sepsis.

answers.text: Start high-dose rituximab immediately in casualty before any specialist consultation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rituximab is a specialist biologic therapy requiring dermatological assessment, staging, and screening for contraindications. It is never initiated in casualty without specialist involvement. Your role is supportive care and urgent referral.

answers.text: Reassure the patient and arrange outpatient review in one month with no fluid or nutritional assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A one-month delay with no supportive care is dangerous. Extensive pemphigus erosions can lead to fatal fluid loss and sepsis within days if not managed actively. This patient needs urgent inpatient supportive care and prompt dermatology referral.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: extensive pemphigus erosions behave like partial-thickness burns. Primary management = non-adherent dressings + fluid monitoring + nutrition + infection watch + analgesic mouthwash + short bridging prednisolone → then urgent referral. Never use adhesive tape on fragile skin.

Correct — primary management before referral treats the erosions like burns: non-adherent wound care, fluid/electrolyte replacement, nutritional support, infection surveillance, a bridging corticosteroid, and urgent specialist referral.
